items.question: How do you see the significance of Meta’s open-sourcing of Llama 2 for people building AI applications?
items.object: Meta’s open-sourcing of Llama 2
items.answer: In AI, when we talk about several core elements, we often mention compute, algorithms, and data. For users interested in AI, I think the most important is really algorithms—for example, all kinds of models and so on. In 2012, Alex Krizhevsky’s AlexNet made us realize that performance in computer vision had improved by a huge margin, opening up many possibilities for different applications. Natural language is the most common way we interact today, just as we’re doing a podcast. So under these circumstances, how to have a good model that can better understand language is a pain point shared by many applications. Llama is, we could say, among the most user-friendly open-source models we see globally today, and probably among the very best in terms of quality as well. The benefit of open source is that everyone can use it as a foundation for building their own higher-level applications without too much pressure, whether financial pressure or considerations such as data security.

items.question: How do you assess the trade-off between using closed-source models and hosting your own model as your application grows?
items.object: Closed-source versus self-hosted models as an application grows
items.answer: At present, if we set aside other business factors and look purely at cost, closed-source models are actually quite inexpensive when I first use them. For example, as a hobbyist, many of us now use ChatGPT and so on to polish documents, draft an email, and the like. In that case, because I don’t need to build a huge cluster myself to run these models, I simply pay for however much I use, so the cost is relatively low. As my application matures and my scale grows, I often encounter two challenges with closed-source models. The first is that a model needs to serve all the different ways the entire world uses it, yet it is a single model—or a small number of models in what we call a mixture-of-experts ensemble. In that situation, it may not be that suitable for an application in my vertical domain, so there may be a ceiling on fit. On the other hand, when the scale of my business or requirements increases, a customized—or, in English, self-hosted—model can increasingly have a better cost-benefit ratio. So once companies reach a certain point, they often start considering whether they need to build their own model, for two reasons. One is that their own application scenarios may perform better with a specialized model. The other is that, from a cost-benefit perspective, the scale is sufficient to support having a model of their own.

items.answer: Another related factor is that AI is beginning to assist with more decision-making in companies. items.question: How do you understand what open source means in practice?
items.object: Open source
items.answer: We can use Apple and Android as an example. Apple’s logic is basically: I have a very good operating system called iOS, and if you use an iPhone, you get to use it. But if you want to modify it yourself, sorry—that’s very difficult. Android says, no problem, right? There are many phone manufacturers; you might want to buy this phone or that phone. I put all of the operating system’s source code out there. If you understand Java, compilation, and embedded systems, you can take my complete operating-system code, and you do not have to write it all again from scratch; you can deploy it. Of course, that does not mean someone without a computer science background—for example, a writer—can also put this thing on their phone. There is still a technical threshold. But it lowers the threshold for rebuilding that operating system. Although open source sounds like a very technical term in everyday life, a great many internet technologies today are built on an open-source model. For example, in servers, we may have heard of an operating system called Linux. We generally do not use it on personal computers; we use Windows and Mac. But Linux is the operating system used by the vast majority of servers. On phones, Android is open source, right? And, for example, the concept we often heard about in the past few years, cloud native: its basic components, such as Kubernetes, are also an ecosystem built entirely on open source.

items.question: How do you understand internet companies’ willingness to support and release open-source software?
items.object: Internet companies’ economic rationale for supporting open-source software
items.answer:
Because every company has its own considerations to some extent, I may not be able to describe it very accurately. Basically, what I find interesting today is that many internet companies are open-sourcing things. The most insightful article I have read on this was written very early on, in the 1990s, by Joel Spolsky, the founder of Stack Overflow. It was called “Strategy Letter V,” or “The Economics of Open Source Software.” He explained that open source can, to a certain extent, be understood using concepts from traditional economics. Open-source software and the labor involved in application development are complements. As software becomes increasingly available, training our engineers to use that software and iterate on top of it becomes less costly. It is a bit like printer companies being willing to make printers very cheap because they can make money from ink cartridges.

With open-source software—or applications on the internet—we make the price of the open-source part of the software cheaper. Rather than selling software, sharing open-source software raises overall development efficiency and lowers development costs. Ultimately, economically, that is net positive. So from this perspective, companies—especially internet companies—generally adopt relatively supportive policies toward open source.

We have seen a very interesting phenomenon: thirty years ago, people might have thought Microsoft was very opposed to open source. But in the past decade or so, Microsoft made a 180-degree shift from a very closed attitude. For example, it acquired and supports GitHub, and it open-sourced the code-editing system formerly called Visual Studio, now called VS Code. Of course, we cannot evaluate Microsoft’s business, but for the community as a whole, this is a very good kind of forward momentum.

items.question: How do you see Llama 2’s contribution to innovation in the large-model industry?
items.object: Llama 2’s contribution to innovation in large models
items.answer: I think that in every new field, the most important thing is to let everyone get to play. If we look at OpenAI, one thing it did incredibly well was that after it released its API, a huge number of experiments in higher-level applications emerged. But if people want to go deeper and say, “I want to see what technical innovation is possible in large models themselves; if I want to have a large model of my own, how should I iterate on it?” then a closed-source model is relatively hard to work with. Llama’s emergence makes it easier for everyone to fine-tune within the framework of such a model and conduct more exploration. For people doing research or algorithms, opening up the black box to see what it looks like inside, then tuning it, changing it, changing it again—that model is always a source of further innovation. So I think Llama 2 has essentially opened this mysterious black box and said, “Look, it can all be used.” One thing I think is different about Llama 2 from many earlier AI models is that previously, people may not have depended so heavily on the open availability of model parameters. Why? For earlier computer vision models and so on, even a university research institution with two or three GPUs could train one in a week. But with large models, we suddenly find that even if the code is available, the model still requires massive amounts of data and compute to train. Open-sourcing code alone is still insufficient. No small research institution or company can invest, for example, tens of millions to train such a model. Llama says: I already have a pretrained model here, and you can fine-tune it. With what is called fine-tuning, the cost of experimenting with and improving large models suddenly comes down. I think that is enormously helpful to the whole industry.

items.question: Why do you think open-sourcing a model like Llama 2 can bring a broader developer community together to improve it?
items.object: Open source as a way to build developer communities
items.answer: There is a saying in open source: “put money on the table.” When more people can benefit, they are more willing to gather together and push the thing forward. This pattern has also occurred in many other software fields. For example, why could open-source operating systems like Linux succeed? Because people felt they could use them more easily, and they were also willing to contribute back. Earlier commercial operating systems such as Xerox and HP-UX were closed source. There were two aspects: first, the barrier to using them was relatively high; second, if I wanted to contribute back, unless I became an employee of that company, there was no way for me to do so. Therefore their developer communities were relatively small. The database field is similar. One thing I used to boast about at Alibaba and major internet companies was that they built their own databases, moving away from the old mainframe-style big databases and building databases in a more internet-oriented way. They were basically built on open-source databases such as MySQL and PostgreSQL, rather than traditional databases such as IBM DB2 or Oracle. This is likewise a trend that open source has brought about in every field.

items.question: How do you see an open-source AI provider’s responsibility for preventing misuse of a model such as Llama?
items.object: Open-source AI providers’ responsibility for preventing misuse of models such as Llama
items.answer: As far as I know, Facebook’s current terms of use for Llama do not specify who can and cannot use it, because this is really somewhat beyond what an open-source provider is capable of handling. I can say, “You must not use it for inhumane things,” but after all, I am not a law-enforcement agency. I think technical matters should be left to technology, and we trust that our society already has courts and law-enforcement agencies to monitor these matters. AI is not actually different from other things. It is like buying a kitchen knife: I also know that the store selling kitchen knives cannot control whether that knife will ultimately be used to hurt someone. But because society itself has a safety system, it can prevent these things. I may be an optimist.

items.question: How do you assess small teams’ prospects for technical innovation in the competition over large AI models?
items.object: Talent and the prospects for small teams in large-model innovation
items.answer: From the technology perspective, I think it is entirely a competition for talent. Just as in computer vision ten years ago, Jeffrey Hinton, Ilya Sutskever, and Alex Krizhevsky—the three of them—were a very small research team able to produce world-renowned results. To a certain extent, innovation does not require a large-scale industrialized approach; often it is just one or two very smart people. This is also why internet companies use open source and similar approaches to attract talent. In that respect, I actually have a relatively positive view of small teams and small companies creating innovative things. Large companies often have many resources, but because their resources must be allocated across many existing businesses due to their own commercial paths, they are not necessarily the best soil for innovation. That is why we see excellent researchers and technical leaders starting companies.

items.question: How do you understand large companies’ commercial advantages in the AI market?
items.object: Large companies’ commercial advantages in applying AI
items.answer: I think large companies should not be underestimated because of their existing business scenarios. There is a saying today—perhaps not entirely correct, and debatable—that AI itself is not a business. For example, I can happily chat with ChatGPT, but the business of chatting is more about better editing documents, editing, advertising, and so on. In other words, AI itself is not a business; it needs to combine with a business to create value. At that point, large companies are naturally built on a very powerful business foundation. Let’s take an example: the rumor today is that Microsoft will release Copilot features in Office that help with editing. Although we do not know for sure, everyone can imagine that if Office had this, we would use it very comfortably, right? Last year, there was an excellent startup called Jasper, which helped people with document editing and so forth. But customer acquisition costs were relatively high for it. Microsoft can say: look, aren’t you already using Office? Haven’t you been using it for years, even decades? I’ll add a feature to it. That is a capability large companies have today: based on their own businesses plus AI innovation, they may be able to steamroll the whole thing in a mechanized way. So I think both small and large companies have advantages in this field. Small companies say, look, I’m more flexible, like guerrillas, more agile and able to get things done. Large companies say, my overall capability for large-scale, organized operations is stronger.

items.question: Why do you see application-driven development as crucial to AI creating greater value?
items.object: Application-driven development as the next source of AI value
items.answer: I think that may be due to my own experience. I started in research, and amid this wave in which everyone rushed toward AI research, I took a path that was not wrong but went against the trend: moving backward from algorithms toward systems, engineering, and products. One thing I feel very strongly is that for an emerging technology, people always go through a period of being very excited by it, of hype. Then, just like the hype curve Gartner often draws, once it reaches the peak of hype, it has to fall for a while before it can move forward steadily. Through all kinds of iteration, people gradually calibrate and come to understand its true capability boundaries. Once those boundaries are established and we move forward steadily, what is really needed is the process of combining the technology with real products. That is application-driven development. So I think understanding needs on the application side is the most crucial point if AI is to create greater value next.

items.question: Where do you think AI applications have the greatest potential to create value today?
items.object: AI applications that improve productivity
items.answer: I think it may be something that gradually creates value in many places. The direction in which AI can provide the most value today may be called productivity. Our earlier hype was the belief that AI could replace all human labor. We have found that it is not really like that. Another phrase people often hear today is, “People who understand AI will replace people who do not understand AI.” What that means is that AI can improve our productivity in doing things today. Take our own company as an example. We have many engineers, and basically everyone has GitHub Copilot to help write code. In my actual coding experience, about 40 percent of the code I write today is written with Copilot’s help. It does not write especially ingenious code or code that requires a great deal of thought, but things such as calling an API, or making a small variation on a section I have already written—these so-called common logistics pieces of code—it can write. Doubling efficiency is a good thing, but it cannot completely replace me. It simply improves my efficiency. In more traditional fields, for example, after a company gets a new employee, it needs to conduct onboarding training. One thing everyone encounters is: wow, all the documents are scattered everywhere, and nobody knows where to find the most useful information for the employee during training. These are places where AI may improve productivity.

items.question: How do you think product builders should respond to customers’ needs?

items.answer: Teaching customers how to behave does not really make sense. items.question: How do you think about the business economics of training costs versus inference costs for large models?
items.object: The economics of training and inference costs for large models
items.answer: Training costs can only ultimately be recouped when you sell the application; they are fixed costs. Inference costs grow linearly with the business. For example, Jasper: the more people use it, the more it earns, and today its inference cost comes from calling the OpenAI API; its inference costs rise as well. So that is more of a linear-growth relationship. Therefore, although inference costs are large in volume, they are a simpler, more direct model that people can understand: I only need to ensure that I have a sufficient profit margin. Training is more like an all-in bet, or an investment in the future. If I invest, say, more than 60 million to train a model, I have to think, “This model, it better be good,” so that I can recoup that money in more applications in the future. Today, in the large-model startup field, we see this situation: people are very enthusiastic about large models, but there is also some concern that we are investing in the future. items.question: How do you think about the problems your company needs to solve to help enterprises use AI?
items.object: System efficiency and human efficiency in enterprise AI adoption
items.answer: What we are doing now is basically helping enterprises solve two problems. The first is system cost. For example, after I buy a whole bunch of machines, it is a bit like saying I bought or operate a shopping center: how do I use my limited real estate to handle enough foot traffic and generate enough revenue? That is a very typical systems problem. The second problem enterprises face today is a people problem. AI experts are still relatively scarce, even though many people are rapidly learning AI. It may take a process like three or four decades ago, when people said computer science education had to start from childhood; for everyone to learn AI will take time. Talent is a major problem. I think that is a very important point for unlocking more potential later. So, on one hand, improve system efficiency; on the other, improve human efficiency. Those are our two premises in general.

items.question: How do you decide which parts of building enterprise AI applications your company should take on?
items.object: The scope of Jia's company's services for enterprises building AI applications
items.answer: If we divide it into layers, at the very bottom there are servers and IDC, which we call IaaS, Infrastructure as a Service. Today, cloud-service providers and so on do that very well, so we do not need to build our own clusters. In the middle there is a layer called Platform as a Service. That is basically how to help users better build a machine-learning platform, and how to manage the many applications of open-source models or models they fine-tune themselves. This platform is where we put a great deal of effort. Previously, I and our co-founders worked on AI frameworks such as Caffe and PyTorch, and on cloud-native frameworks such as Kubernetes, so we have relatively extensive experience there. For this fine-tuning, we use a more principled approach to tell them that they may not need to write a pile of messy code. items.answer: Because I have not done fundamental research for a long time, I may not be completely accurate about this. But from a systems perspective, we do feel that transformers are not a particularly good architecture. At least our brain probably doesn’t use a transformer. It is somewhat brute force. It says: look, how do I make this model remember more? I give it a longer context. This is a bit like having a new colleague join. This is not the best kind of model. There’s gotta be something that’s better. So from the model perspective, I am quite looking forward to more mature alternatives above or outside transformers.
